headline: Harvard's $699 startup bootcamp offers AI avatars of its instructors for feedback
summary: Harvard Business School's new 8-week Foundry bootcamp for entrepreneurs uses AI avatars from HeyGen to provide personalized feedback during practice sessions. Students generally like the virtual instructors, despite some finding them 'creepy'.
details: Harvard Business School is expanding its reach by integrating AI avatars into its new 8-week, $699 HBS Foundry bootcamp for entrepreneurs. These avatars, created by the startup HeyGen, are designed to provide individual feedback to participants.

While the program includes weekly live sessions with human instructors, the AI avatars are responsible for delivering feedback during crucial practice pitches and board meetings. This blended approach aims to offer a more guided and personalized learning experience.

A New York Times reporter tested the system, pitching to an AI-generated copy of Flybridge Capital co-founder Jeff Bussgang. Both the real and virtual Bussgang were unimpressed by her idea, with the AI version notably displaying a "frozen smile" during the pitch.

Project director Katharina Rings initially envisioned a simpler chatbot component, but student feedback from a trial version indicated a preference for a more structured and guided interaction. This led to the development of the current avatar system.

Despite some college students expressing negative sentiments towards AI, participants in the Foundry bootcamp have reportedly reacted positively to the avatars. Jeff Bussgang acknowledged his digital counterpart is "a little creepy" but confirmed his students "love it."

headline_marked: [[Inherent's AI agent outperforms Anthropic & OpenAI]] at replicating research with a fraction of the model size
headline: Inherent's AI agent outperforms Anthropic & OpenAI at replicating research with a fraction of the model size
summary: London-based Inherent's Faraday agent replicated scientific papers, beating larger frontier models like Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 using a 27-billion-parameter model.
details: Inherent, a London AI lab founded by Google DeepMind alumni, announced its AI agent, Faraday, has outperformed much larger models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Faraday successfully reproduced the findings of published scientific papers without prior knowledge of the answers.

This achievement is notable as Faraday runs on a comparatively tiny model called Qwen 3.6, with just 27 billion parameters. This is significantly smaller than frontier-scale systems like Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 and OpenAI's GPT-5.5, which it surpassed.

The startup's success metric went beyond mere accuracy; Inherent aimed for Faraday to demonstrate "research taste." This involves an instinct for identifying which experiments are valuable and how to design them effectively.

To instill this intangible "taste," Inherent utilizes reinforcement learning, a training method that rewards the AI for positive outcomes rather than explicit rule-following. This approach is expected to generalize better for future scientific contributions.

Inherent's long-term goal is to build an AI scientist agent capable of discovering new scientific knowledge, not just verifying existing results. This focus guides their development choices, including using existing tools like OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Codex for coding tasks.

The company also aims to create collaborative agents that challenge assumptions rather than simply confirming user biases. They envision an AI teammate that explores curiosities and presents novel experimental results.

Inherent recently emerged from stealth with a $50 million seed round and operates from a London office in King's Cross. The company's founders include DeepMind alumni, contributing to London's growing AI hub.

The startup plans to expand its headcount to 20-25 by year-end, attracting talent in the competitive AI landscape. This growth positions Inherent as an appealing destination for researchers, including those from DeepMind.
